newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM mum on polls despite Okinawa resolution.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM mum on polls despite Okinawa resolution.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday played down talk of snap elections despite the release of key economic data and the resolution of a dispute with Okinawa over U.S. bases -- the two factors he earlier cited as reasons for delaying his decision on polls.

Hashimoto will visit Okinawa next week to underscore the government's commitment to easing the burden of a lopsided concentration of U.S. bases there, then meet with coalition partners to work out an election calendar, his spokesman said.

The thorniest political problem faced by Hashimoto's government eased on Friday when Okinawa's governor agreed to take steps to renew leases for U.S. military bases on the island, ending a bitter one-year standoff with Tokyo.
Earlier, citing data released by the Economic Planning Agency (EPA), the government said the economy was still improving despite a slip backwards in the three months to June.
Gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key gauge of the economy's health -- fell a real 0.7 percent in the April-June period from the previous quarter.

Although the figures mark a drop from a revised 2.9 percent quarter-on-quarter or an annualised 12.2 percent growth in the January-March period, analysts and government officials said pressure for a big public stimulus package had faded.
The easing of major political and economic hurdles appeared to ease the way for general elections, which are not mandated until July 1997.
But Hashimoto dismissed talk that he would promptly move to call polls and criticised rampant media speculation that he had already set October 20 as an election date.
"We are of course far from a solution to the Okinawa problem," Hashimoto said in response to a question about polls.
"The constant reports of a early elections made Okinawans anxious that all discussions (to solve their problems) would go down the drain," he said.

Hashimoto said he would fly to Okinawa on Tuesday with a team of ministers to back up his pledge this week to shrink U.S. bases and set up a five billion yen ($45.8 million) fund for the economic development of Okinawa prefecture, the poorest in Japan with average income half the level of Tokyo's.

The pledge eased the way for Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota to end his refusal to renew leases for U.S. facilities. Ota took the hardline stance following the rape last year of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, a case that re-ignited anti-base protests on the island.

In addition to showing sensitivity to Okinawan concerns, Hashimoto, who is also president of the Liberal Democratic Party has had to defer to the LDP's coalition partners, the Social Democratic Party and Sakigake, both of whom oppose early polls.

Social Democratic Party head Tomiichi Murayama and Sakigake chief Shoichi Ide, whose small parties are struggling to merge before elections, have criticised LDP leaks to the local media treating the electoral calendar as a done deal.

The three party heads are expected to discuss election timing on September 19, but few analysts expect feverish election speculation -- or politicians calls for a heavy dose of public spending ahead of national polls -- to subside.

Many in the LDP want to get elections out of the way well before an unpopular rise in a consumption tax to five percent from three percent next April -- one of the few clear policy issues to emerge in the run up to the campaign.
